title: Umar's letter on judging
hook: judge with understanding, treat both sides equally, the claimant brings proof
tomorrow: a stranger isn't your brother. so what is he to you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr asked the crowd: correct me. After him, Umar led, and he wrote down how to judge between people.

Two friends, one argument, and both are texting you their side. Each version is airtight. Each one ends: you agree, right? Being the judge feels like a trap: agree with one and lose the other, stay quiet and lose both. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote a letter for exactly this seat, to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a judge he had appointed.
screen: `TWO SIDES, BOTH AIRTIGHT.` → `YOU AGREE, RIGHT?` → `A LETTER FOR THE JUDGE'S SEAT.`

segments.voice: The letter is short and packed. Judging, Umar says, is a firm duty. Understand what's brought to you, because a right that isn't carried out does no good. Then the line at its heart: treat people as equals in how you look at them, where you seat them and how you judge them, so the powerful don't hope for your favor and the weak don't despair of your fairness. The one who makes a claim must bring the proof; the one who denies takes an oath. Don't let a judgment you made yesterday stop you from returning to what's right after you've thought again, because returning to the truth is better than staying in a wrong. And understanding, understanding, he repeats, when a case isn't plainly settled in the Qur'an or the Sunna. Last: keep anger and irritation out of the courtroom. Now bring it into the group chat. Equal in how you look means one friend doesn't get the warmer face. The claimant brings proof means the loudest text doesn't win. And the line about yesterday means even your first opinion can change. Umar wrote for courts. It fits a kitchen table, a team, a club, anywhere two people need someone to be fair.
screen: `A RIGHT MUST BE CARRIED OUT.` · `THE SAME FACE TO BOTH SIDES.` · `THE CLAIMANT BRINGS PROOF.` · `YESTERDAY'S RULING CAN CHANGE.` · then, large: `EQUAL BEFORE YOU.`

segments.voice: Listen for two sounds, one on your left and one on your right. Give each the same attention and the same patience, turn by turn. When one pulls at you more, come back to the other.
screen: `ONE SOUND ON EACH SIDE.` · `THE SAME ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Umar's letter on judging: to Abu Musa, a judge, on treating both sides as equals and letting proof, not volume, decide.
The line to keep: equal before you, in your face and in your fairness. Day 1643, heard out.

screen: `DAY 1643 COUNTS.` → `SERMONS AND LETTERS · 3 OF 6.` → `TOMORROW: SO WHAT IS A STRANGER TO YOU?`

howItsDone: Umar's letter to Abu Musa is taught in Islamic law and judging as a guide to a judge's conduct; its line on the claimant's proof echoes a principle Muslim jurists apply in courts.

myth: Umar tells a judge to stand by his first ruling no matter what
returning to the truth after thinking again is better than staying in a wrong.

and the one who denies takes an oath.

fork.setup: your two kids each say the other broke the lamp. one is crying loudly; the other is quiet. what would Umar's letter have you do first?
options: give both the same calm face, and ask what each can show.
comfort the loud one first; the tears show who's hurt.
punish both the same so nobody feels singled out.
fork.reveal: equal in how you look at them, and proof from the one who claims. the loudest side doesn't win, and the same punishment isn't the same as a fair hearing.

original.note: Arabic: al-fahm al-fahm, understanding, understanding: Umar's repeated word to his judge.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fair judge just splits the difference.
what it means: the same face to both sides, proof from the one who claims, and freedom to correct your own ruling.
what a scholar hears: Umar's letter to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, kept by al-Daraqutni and others and explained at length by Ibn Qayyim; scholars discuss its chain.
guess: Umar's instructions to a judge on fairness and proof
a law code that fixed penalties for crimes
a letter naming who would rule after Umar

chat.says: two tutors fighting over the library room. both swear they booked it. both want me on their side
options: Same face to both, then ask who can show the booking. Proof decides, not the louder voice.
Side with whoever asked first. Being decisive matters more than every detail.
Split the room down the middle. Fairness means everyone just gets half.
chat.meaning: Umar told his judge to treat both sides equally in face and fairness, and to let the one who claims bring the proof.

Umar ibn al-Khattab.meaning: a companion of the Prophet who led after Abu Bakr

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.meaning: a companion Umar appointed as a judge

Sunna.meaning: the Prophet's example: what he said and did

sources.ref: Umar ibn al-Khattab's letter to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari on judging (al-Daraqutni, Sunan, Kitab fi al-aqdiya; al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra; commentary in Ibn Qayyim, I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in)
sources.work: Letter of Umar to Abu Musa

notes: Umar's letter paraphrased: judging a firm duty and followed practice; understand what is brought; a right not carried out is of no use; equality in gaze, seating and justice so the noble don't covet bias and the weak don't despair; proof on the claimant, oath on the denier; returning to the truth after reconsidering; al-fahm al-fahm where Qur'an and Sunna are silent; avoid anger and irritation.
